title: Application-aware egress proxy and DNS resolution playbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for migrating on-prem / VPC private deployments to an application-aware egress model with deterministic DNS resolution. Focus is on minimizing blast radius during upgrades, avoiding split-horizon complexity where possible, and providing a Terraform-first implementation path for customers who run Redwood Private in their VPCs or on-prem clusters.

Scope:
- Private deployments (VPC and on-prem) for Redwood Private control/data plane components and customer model-serving pods.
- Networking elements: private DNS resolution, egress architecture (proxy vs NAT), firewall rules, k8s NetworkPolicies, and Terraform module design.
- Excludes: non-HTTP protocols that require special tunneling (Kafka, raw TCP streaming) — covered separately.

Assumptions:
- Customers run Kubernetes clusters (K8s v1.24+) for Redwood workloads or use cloud VMs behind ASG equivalents.
- There is an existing VPC-level NAT gateway(s) or on-prem edge firewall appliance.
- Team has basic Terraform state management (remote state, locking).

Goals:
1) Provide deterministic DNS resolution for internal services and model artifact stores (avoid stale cached records).
2) Route all egress through application-aware proxy layer for allowlisting, auth, and telemetry.
3) Keep Kubernetes NetworkPolicy simple: block-by-default, explicit allow to proxy and required cloud APIs.
4) Deliver Terraform modules and upgrade/runbook that minimize customer downtime and make rollback straightforward.

High-level design:
- DNS: Use conditional-forwarding/conditional-forwarders for Kubernetes CoreDNS to forward specific domains (eg storage.redwood.internal, models.redwood) to customer private resolver or to an internal resolver pool. Set short TTLs (30-60s) for dynamic endpoints (model-serving replicas) and longer TTLs for stable endpoints (control plane).
- Egress: Introduce an application-aware forward proxy deployed as a DaemonSet (sidecar or node-proxy option) or as a central proxy cluster. All pods allowed to egress must go through proxy via iptables redirect or Kyverno admission to inject env vars.
- NAT fallback: If proxy unavailable, traffic should fail closed for controlled services; non-critical telemetry may fallback to NAT with strict rate-limits.
- Firewall: Use minimal L4 rules at VPC edge and beef up L7 at proxy layer. VPC firewall rules should only permit outbound to proxy endpoints and to cloud provider control plane IPs.

DNS strategy details:
- CoreDNS config options to include:
  - stubDomains / forward plugin entries for: models.redwood.internal -> internal-resolver:5353
  - cached response TTLs: set `ttl` plugin or ResponsePolicy TTLs where supported
  - health check path for resolver (http://resolver:8080/health) for automated failover in the Control Plane

- Example Corefile snippet (in terraform-k8s addon):

  .:53 {
      errors
      health
      kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
          pods insecure
          fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
      }
      forward . /etc/resolv.conf
      forward models.redwood.internal internal-dns-01:5353 internal-dns-02:5353
      cache 30
      loop
  }

- Operational notes:
  - TTL: 30s for model endpoints that may be rebalanced across AZs; 300s for control plane endpoints.
  - Monitor NXDOMAIN spikes — correlate with failed egress or DNS timeouts.

Egress architecture options (tradeoffs):
1) Centralized proxy cluster (HA)
   - Pros: single place for auth, metrics, and TLS termination; easier to maintain client config
   - Cons: additional egress latency; scaling requires capacity planning
2) Node-local sidecars / iptables redirect
   - Pros: lower latency, avoids central bottleneck
   - Cons: more complex lifecycle and upgrade story, requires careful iptables handling to avoid port exhaustion
3) Hybrid: node-local for high-throughput telemetry, central proxy for control plane and 3rd-party APIs

Recommendation: Start with hybrid model for largest customers, default to centralized proxy for self-hosted early adopters to simplify rollout.

Proxy implementation details:
- Preferred proxy: Envoy or OTEL-aware HTTP forward proxy (we have a reference envoy-filter config in infra repo).
- Authentication: mTLS between pods and proxy, proxy authenticates to external services with per-route credentials stored in K8s secrets (or cloud KMS).
- Rate-limiting: implement token-bucket per-namespace to prevent noisy-tenant issues.

Terraform module notes (customer-facing module structure):
- Module name: redwood_private_networking
- Inputs (selected):
  - proxy_mode (string): centralized | node-local | hybrid
  - dns_forwarders (list): ["10.0.2.4:5353", "10.0.3.4:5353"]
  - nat_gateways_enabled (bool)
  - egress_allowed_cidrs (list): cloud control plane cidrs, k8s registry ranges
  - firewall_management_account (string)
- Outputs (selected):
  - proxy_endpoints (list)
  - corefile_config (string)

Example usage snippet (terraform):

module "redwood_private_networking" {
  source = "git::https://github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules.git//networking?ref=v0.12.0"
  proxy_mode = "hybrid"
  dns_forwarders = ["10.1.0.5:5353","10.1.0.6:5353"]
  nat_gateways_enabled = true
  egress_allowed_cidrs = ["10.0.0.0/8","0.0.0.0/0"]
}

Terraform upgrade considerations:
- State migration: split `redwood_networking` into submodules (dns, proxy, firewall) so upgrades can be applied independently.
- Use `terraform plan -target=module.redwood_private_networking.proxy` during staged rollout.
- Locking: ensure Terraform state locking with DynamoDB or equivalent to avoid concurrent apply races.

Firewall rules (VPC level) guidance:
- Default egress: deny. Create explicit outbound rules:
  - allow outbound to proxy endpoint CIDRs (TCP 8080/8443)
  - allow outbound to cloud provider control plane (kube-api endpoints)
  - restricted ports for metrics/monitoring collectors (TCP 8125, 9090)
- Ingress: only allow inbound from known customer admin IP ranges and internal load balancers.

Kubernetes NetworkPolicy recommendations:
- Default: deny all ingress/egress.
- Minimal allow rules per namespace:
  - allow egress to `kube-system` DNS and to proxy `redwood-proxy.ns.svc.cluster.local`
  - allow egress to model artifact storage endpoints (by CIDR or DNS via proxy)
  - example YAML (flat text):

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-egress
  namespace: redwood
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: redwood-system
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: redwood-proxy
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080

Upgrade/runbook (stepwise):
1) Pre-checks (2 days ahead):
   - Inventory: list clusters, NAT gateway configurations, CoreDNS versions (document per-customer in spreadsheet).
   - Backups: export terraform state and CoreDNS ConfigMaps.
   - Smoke test harness: ensure we have a Canary namespace with synthetic traffic to verify egress proxy behaviour.
2) Deploy proxy in "observe-only" mode:
   - Deploy with metrics and `allow_all_backends=false` but do not redirect traffic. Collect metrics for 24 hours.
3) Inject DNS forwards to internal resolver in a single dev cluster: verify resolution and TTL behaviour.
4) Enable iptables redirect for small percentage of namespaces (canary) using admission label `egress-canary=true`.
5) Gradually increase percent and monitor:
   - watch for 502/504 spikes, increase in DNS NXDOMAIN, port exhaustion in nodes.
6) If errors > threshold (5% 5m error rate), rollback to previous iptables rules and scale proxy.

Rollback plan:
- Immediate rollback: remove iptables redirect/restore kube-proxy rules to previous state using saved ipset snapshots.
- Terraform-level rollback: re-apply previous revision tag to networking modules, then re-deploy CoreDNS configmap from backup.

Testing and observability:
- Metrics to collect:
  - proxy_request_latency_by_route
  - dns_query_latency
  - dns_nxdomain_rate
  - node_ephemeral_port_utilization
  - terraform_apply_duration (CI metric)
- Synthetic checks:
  - call control plane endpoints via proxy and direct NAT, validate identity headers and response times
  - DNS resolution test: query models.redwood.internal from multiple nodes and compare TTL/answers

Checklist for customers before enabling egress policy:
- Confirm list of 3rd-party endpoints and required ports (provide CSV template)
- Confirm KMS / secret rotation plan for proxy credentials
- Confirm observability endpoints and retention requirements

Open questions / risks:
- How do we support UDP-based model-serving telemetry (OTLP/metrics over UDP)? (Currently plan: route via node-local forwarder or dedicated NAT path)
- Port exhaustion on older instance types during iptables redirect spikes — require pressure testing per-customer
- Customers with strict split-horizon DNS policies may require a managed DNS-forwarder appliance; we need a hardened reference deployment for those cases.

Next actions / owners:
- Maya: draft CoreDNS ConfigMap generator in terraform module (due 2024-11-20)
- Samir: prototype Envoy proxy config for model artifact signing (due 2024-11-28)
- Jordan: author automated test harness (k8s job + terraform) for canary rollout (due 2024-12-05)

Notes-to-self / rough todos (informal):
- add example iptables restore script to infra repo
- create jira epic JIRA-5000 to track rollout across top-10 customers
- get legal ok for TLS termination default policy

Appendix: quick commands
- Dump CoreDNS configmap: kubectl -n kube-system get configmap coredns -o yaml > coredns-backup-$(date +%F).yaml
- Snapshot ipset (for rollback): sudo ipset save > /var/tmp/ipset-snapshot-$(hostname)-$(date +%s).txt
- Terraform targeted plan: terraform plan -target=module.redwood_private_networking.proxy -out=plan.tfplan

End of draft.
